blocks.text:
Design a coffee vending machine that serves multiple drinks, espresso, cappuccino, latte, each brewed from a recipe of shared ingredients: water, milk, coffee beans, and sugar. A customer pays, picks a drink with optional add-ons like extra milk, and the machine brews it, returns change, and tracks ingredient levels for the operator.

This looks like the snack vending machine, but two twists change the design. A drink consumes several shared ingredients at once, so availability is a multi resource, all or nothing reservation. And add-ons stack on a base drink, extra milk on a cappuccino with extra sugar, which is the textbook home of the Decorator pattern.

  • Actors: customers buying drinks, and operators refilling ingredients and tuning recipes
  • Scope: one machine, several outlets sharing one ingredient inventory, cash with a payment abstraction, in memory
  • Goal: a design where new drinks and new add-ons are data and decorators, never edits

The snack machine sells one item from one shelf. The coffee machine builds a product from shared parts, and that difference drives every design choice here.
blocks.content:
Design a coffee vending machine that serves multiple drinks, espresso, cappuccino, latte, each brewed from a recipe of shared ingredients: water, milk, coffee beans, and sugar. A customer pays, picks a drink with optional add-ons like extra milk, and the machine brews it, returns change, and tracks ingredient levels for the operator.

This looks like the snack vending machine, but two twists change the design. A drink consumes several shared ingredients at once, so availability is a multi resource, all or nothing reservation. And add-ons stack on a base drink, extra milk on a cappuccino with extra sugar, which is the textbook home of the Decorator pattern.

  • Actors: customers buying drinks, and operators refilling ingredients and tuning recipes
  • Scope: one machine, several outlets sharing one ingredient inventory, cash with a payment abstraction, in memory
  • Goal: a design where new drinks and new add-ons are data and decorators, never edits

The snack machine sells one item from one shelf. The coffee machine builds a product from shared parts, and that difference drives every design choice here.

blocks.text: The machine must support the full journey from payment to a hot cup, plus the operator loop that keeps it stocked.

metadata.alt: Functional requirements at a glance: pay, choose, check, brew, or reject cleanly

items: Accept payment: coins and notes, with a running balance and a payment abstraction for cards later
Serve a menu: espresso, cappuccino, latte, and black coffee, each defined by a recipe
Add-ons: extra milk, extra sugar, extra shot, stackable on any base drink
Check before brewing: verify balance and reserve every required ingredient, or reject naming what is missing
Brew and dispense: pour the drink and return exact change
Cancel: full refund any time before brewing starts
Operator: refill ingredients, read levels, add or reprice recipes

blocks.text: Ingredient accounting is the honour of this machine: a cup poured must always equal ingredients deducted, even with several outlets pouring at once.
Every millilitre and gram is deducted exactly once, and only for drinks actually served. A rejected order deducts nothing.
Multiple outlets share one inventory. Two lattes must never both be approved when only one latte worth of milk remains.
A new drink is one recipe entry; a new add-on is one decorator class. The machine core never changes for menu work.
Selection and reservation are constant time over a handful of ingredients; brewing time dominates and is hardware bound.
Recipes are data, states are small classes, and money code is isolated, so each concern changes independently.
Coffee machine scope swings from a single button kettle to a cafe robot, so pin it down.

items: Menu: how many drinks, and are add-ons like extra shots in scope?
Outlets: one dispensing point, or several pouring concurrently from shared containers?
Payment: cash only, or should the design anticipate cards and wallets?
Recipes: fixed at build time, or operator editable?
Quantities: do we track real units, millilitres and grams, or abstract portions?
Alerts: should low ingredient levels notify the operator?

blocks.text: Assumed answers for this design: four base drinks with three stackable add-ons; three outlets sharing one inventory; cash behind a PaymentStrategy; operator editable recipes; real units in integers; low level alerts noted as an observer extension.
These constraints keep the machine honest and the interview scoped.

items: Money: integer paise, no floating point; prices are per beverage after decoration
Units: ingredients tracked as integers: millilitres for liquids, grams for solids
Reservation rule: all ingredients for a drink are reserved atomically before brewing, or none are
Session: one customer per outlet; outlets contend only on the shared inventory
Change: if exact change is impossible the sale is refused before brewing
State: in memory; the database section defines the persistent schema

blocks.text: The nouns of the problem, each owning exactly one job.

metadata.alt: The core entities and how they connect

items: CoffeeMachine: the context: owns the balance, the current state, and coordinates a purchase
MachineState: an interface with Idle, HasMoney, and Brewing implementations
IngredientInventory: the shared containers, with the atomic all or nothing reserve
Ingredient: an enum: WATER, MILK, BEANS, SUGAR
Recipe: what a drink needs and costs; RecipeBook maps drink types to recipes
Beverage and decorators: a base drink wrapped by add-ons, each adding cost and ingredient needs
PaymentStrategy: how money is collected: cash now, cards later

blocks.text: The ownership story, told with the four relationship kinds.

metadata.alt: Composition, aggregation, association, and the decorator wrap

items: CoffeeMachine composes IngredientInventory and RecipeBook: they are built with the machine and die with it
RecipeBook composes its Recipes: a recipe belongs to exactly one book
Recipe aggregates ingredient amounts: a map of enum to units, shared vocabulary across recipes
A decorator aggregates the beverage it wraps: the wrapped drink exists in its own right
The machine uses a PaymentStrategy per transaction without owning it
States call back into the machine to reach the inventory, the book, and the balance
Idle, HasMoney, and Brewing implement MachineState
BaseBeverage and BeverageDecorator implement Beverage; ExtraMilk and ExtraSugar extend the decorator

blocks.text: One view of the whole design: the state hierarchy runs the session, the decorator hierarchy builds the product, and the inventory guards the shared containers.

metadata.alt: UML class diagram of the coffee vending machine

blocks.text: Reading guide: the open diamond from BeverageDecorator back to Beverage is the decorator loop, a wrapper holding the thing it wraps through the same interface. That one arrow is what makes add-ons stack to any depth.
Three patterns carry the machine, each chosen by a symptom in the problem.
Why needed: selecting a drink before paying must behave differently from selecting after paying, and nothing may interrupt a brew in progress.
Why it is the best choice: the same reasoning as every machine problem: flags multiply and hide transitions; one class per mode keeps every rule local and testable.
What it solves: illegal actions are rejected by construction, and a Cleaning or Maintenance mode later is one new class.

metadata.alt: The session states and their transitions

blocks.text: Why needed: add-ons stack: a cappuccino with extra milk and extra sugar. Subclassing every combination explodes: CappuccinoWithMilk, CappuccinoWithMilkAndSugar, and so on forever.
Why it is the best choice: each decorator wraps any Beverage and adds its own cost and ingredient needs. Combinations are free: wrap in any order, to any depth, no new classes per combination.
What it solves: the combination explosion, and it keeps pricing and ingredient math composable: the final cost and needs are computed by walking the wrappers.

metadata.alt: Decorators stack: each wrapper adds cost and ingredients to the drink inside it

blocks.text: Why needed and what it solves: cash today, cards and UPI tomorrow. One PaymentStrategy interface keeps the machine frozen while payment tech evolves, exactly as in the snack machine.
The RecipeBook is a small factory: it turns a drink type into a configured Recipe. Low ingredient alerts are observers on the inventory, keeping notifications out of the core.
State runs the session, Decorator builds the drink, Strategy takes the money. Three symptoms, three patterns, zero buzzwords.
blocks.content: State runs the session, Decorator builds the drink, Strategy takes the money. Three symptoms, three patterns, zero buzzwords.

blocks.text: Each class in one breath: responsibility, attributes, methods.

items: Responsibility: own the purchase context and delegate every action to the current state
Attributes: state, balance, inventory, recipeBook, pending beverage
Methods: insertMoney(amount), selectDrink(type, addons), dispense(), refund(), plus operator refill and levels
IdleState: accepts money and moves to HasMoney; rejects selection and refund
HasMoneyState: accumulates money; on selection builds the decorated beverage, checks the balance, reserves ingredients atomically, then moves to Brewing
BrewingState: pours the drink, returns change, resets, and goes back to Idle; rejects everything else mid brew
Responsibility: the single guardian of shared stock, with the atomic multi ingredient reserve
Attributes: an EnumMap of Ingredient to units
Methods: tryReserve(needs) checking all then deducting all inside one lock, refill(ingredient, qty), level(ingredient)
Recipe: immutable needs map plus a price
RecipeBook: drink type to recipe, operator editable
BaseBeverage: wraps a recipe as the innermost Beverage
BeverageDecorator and children: add cost and needs on top of whatever they wrap

blocks.text: Three interfaces isolate the three axes of change: session mode, product composition, and payment method.

Why Beverage is the interesting one: both the base drink and every decorator implement it, so the machine holds one Beverage reference and never knows how many wrappers are inside. cost() and needs() recurse through the stack naturally.
Three workflows define the machine: a decorated happy path, a clean ingredient rejection, and two outlets racing on the last milk.
12.1 Happy path: cappuccino with extra milk
blocks.content: 12.1 Happy path: cappuccino with extra milk

metadata.alt: Sequence diagram of a successful decorated purchase

blocks.text: The recipe is fetched, decorated, priced, and only then is the inventory asked to reserve. Reservation happens before any brewing, so a poured cup is always fully paid and fully stocked.

metadata.alt: A latte is rejected for milk; a black coffee succeeds immediately after

blocks.text: The reserve is all or nothing, so the failed latte deducts nothing, and the same customer immediately buys a black coffee that needs no milk. Naming the missing ingredient is a small UX touch interviewers reward.
12.3 Race path: two outlets, last of the milk
blocks.content: 12.3 Race path: two outlets, last of the milk

metadata.alt: The synchronized reserve lets exactly one of two simultaneous lattes win

blocks.text: With 80ml of milk and two 60ml lattes requested simultaneously, the synchronized reserve admits exactly one. The loser gets a clean rejection, and the books still balance.
The purchase pipeline has two gates: money, then ingredients. Both must pass before anything is consumed.

metadata.alt: The purchase flow with its two validation gates

items: The customer inserts money; the machine shows the balance and enters HasMoney
The customer picks a drink and add-ons; the machine builds the decorated beverage
Gate one: the balance must cover the decorated cost
Gate two: tryReserve deducts every required ingredient atomically
The machine brews, pours, and returns change
The machine resets to Idle for the next customer
Balance short: the selection is rejected with the exact shortfall; the customer adds money or cancels
Ingredient short: rejected naming the ingredient; nothing deducted; other drinks remain available
Change impossible: refused before reserving, protecting the customer
Cancel in HasMoney: full refund, back to Idle
Brew hardware fault: reserved ingredients are released back and the customer refunded, the one compensating path

blocks.text: Customers see four methods; operators see three.

metadata.alt: The public API surface for customers and operators

codes.python:
# customer facing
def insert_money(self, amount: int) -> None: ...
def select_drink(self, drink_type: DrinkType, addons: List[AddOn]) -> None: ...
def dispense(self) -> None: ...                        # driven by BrewingState
def refund(self) -> None: ...

# operator facing
def refill(self, ing: Ingredient, units: int) -> None: ...
def levels(self) -> Dict[Ingredient, int]: ...
def add_recipe(self, drink_type: DrinkType, recipe: Recipe) -> None: ...

items: selectDrink: the heart: decorate, price check, atomic reserve, then transition to Brewing
refund: legal in HasMoney; a no op rejection in Idle; refused mid brew
refill and levels: operator loop; refill also clears any low stock alert

blocks.text: Failures are specific, name the cause, and never leave ingredients half deducted.

metadata.alt: The failure categories and their exceptions

items: UnknownDrinkException: a type with no recipe in the book
InvalidAmountException: zero or negative money rejected at the door
IngredientUnavailableException: carries the ingredient name and how much was missing
ChangeUnavailableException: raised before reservation, sale refused safely
InsufficientBalanceException: carries cost and current balance
IllegalStateException: any action attempted in the wrong session state
BrewFailureException: triggers the compensating path: release reserved units, refund the customer
Guarantee: every exception leaves inventory equal to what was actually poured

blocks.text: The shared inventory is the whole concurrency story, and it is a multi resource version of the last item problem.

metadata.alt: The atomic multi ingredient reserve: check all, deduct all, inside one lock

items: Two outlets, one ingredient: both see enough milk, both deduct, stock goes negative
Partial deduction: outlet one takes the milk while outlet two takes the beans, and neither can finish
Refill during reserve: an operator refill interleaving with a reservation

blocks.text: The reserve must check every ingredient and deduct every ingredient as one indivisible step. Locking per ingredient invites deadlock and partial states; one lock on the whole inventory is correct and, with a handful of ingredients, contention free in practice.
release() is the compensating half: if the brewer faults after reservation, the units go back and the books stay true. This reserve and release pair is a miniature transaction.
Menu work is the daily life of a coffee machine, and none of it touches the core.

metadata.alt: Extensions land as recipes, decorators, strategies, and observers

items: New drink: one Recipe entry in the book: pure data, zero code
New add-on: one decorator class declaring its extra cost and needs
New payment method: one PaymentStrategy implementation
Low stock alerts: observers on the inventory, notified inside refill and reserve
Cleaning mode: one new MachineState that rejects customer actions
Cup sizes: a size multiplier on Recipe, or a size decorator, both non invasive

blocks.text: Future enhancements: a touch screen menu, loyalty pricing, and remote telemetry all attach at the edges: presentation observers and pricing decorators, with the brewing core untouched.

metadata.alt: How the coffee machine design maps to SOLID

items: Single Responsibility: inventory counts, recipes describe, decorators price, states sequence, the machine coordinates
Open Closed: drinks, add-ons, payments, and modes all extend without edits
Liskov Substitution: a triple decorated latte is still a Beverage everywhere a Beverage is expected
Interface Segregation: MachineState, Beverage, and PaymentStrategy are each a handful of methods
Dependency Inversion: the machine holds abstractions; concrete states, drinks, and payments are injected or constructed behind factories

blocks.text: The cases that separate a demo from a design.

metadata.alt: The edge cases the design must survive

items: Decorator pushes cost past the balance: the price check runs on the decorated cost, so the rejection names the true total
Ingredient runs out between selection and confirm: tryReserve is the single source of truth at commit time
Two outlets, last of an ingredient: exactly one wins the synchronized reserve
Cancel after reservation but before pouring: release() returns the units and the refund is full
Exact payment: change of zero pays out nothing and completes normally
Recipe edited while a drink is mid brew: the brew holds its own copied needs map, so edits affect only future orders
Same add-on twice: allowed by design: double extra milk simply wraps twice

blocks.text: Everything is constant time over a fixed handful of ingredients and wrappers.

items: selectDrink: O(D) to walk D decorators for cost and needs, plus O(I) to reserve I ingredients; both single digits
tryReserve: O(I) check plus O(I) deduct inside one lock
refill and levels: O(1) and O(I)
dispense: O(1) bookkeeping; brewing time is hardware, not algorithm
O(I): the inventory map
O(R x I): the recipe book over R drinks
O(D): the decorator stack of the current order, freed after pouring

blocks.text: Persist the menu, the stock, and every sale, so a restart loses nothing and the operator sees real consumption.

metadata.alt: Entity relationship diagram for the coffee machine

items: INGREDIENT: live stock with capacity and a low threshold for alerts
RECIPE and RECIPE_NEED: the menu as data: one row per drink, one row per ingredient requirement
SALE: one row per served cup with add-ons, amount, and change: the audit and analytics trail
SALE(created_at): daily sales and peak hour reports
SALE(drink_type): menu popularity, which drives refill planning
RECIPE_NEED(ingredient): which drinks a shortage disables, answered in one query

blocks.text: The sale insert and the ingredient deductions commit together, mirroring the in memory rule: a recorded cup always equals deducted stock.
The follow ups probe the two twists: shared ingredients and decorators.

items: Reservation queue: under heavy contention, queue reserves per outlet for fairness instead of lock racing
Predictive refill: use SALE data to forecast when milk runs out by hour of day
Pre grinding: pipeline the brew stages across outlets when hardware allows
Why Decorator over subclassing: four drinks with three stackable add-ons is dozens of subclasses versus three decorators
Why one inventory lock: per ingredient locks invite deadlock; the critical section is microseconds over four entries
Snack machine versus coffee machine: single resource shelf versus multi resource recipe: the reserve is the difference
A fleet of machines: each is autonomous; stock levels and sales sync to a central service for routing refill staff
Menu pushes: recipes update over the air as data, which is why recipes as data matters
Idempotent sales upload: sale ids prevent double counting on retries

blocks.text: Lead with the two twists, because they are what make this problem not just the snack machine again.

items: Open by contrasting with the snack machine: multi ingredient recipes and stackable add-ons are the new problems
Name the three patterns with reasons: State for the session, Decorator for add-ons, Strategy for payment
Show the decorator stack computing cost and needs by recursion through the wrappers
Walk the two gates in selectDrink: decorated cost against balance, then the atomic reserve
Spell out tryReserve: check all, deduct all, one lock, and why per ingredient locks invite deadlock
Show release() as the compensating transaction for brew failures
Mention recipes as data: menu changes ship without code
Close with the outlets race: exactly one latte from 80ml of milk, provably

blocks.text: Each choice has a credible alternative worth naming.
26.1 Decorator versus flags on the order
blocks.content: 26.1 Decorator versus flags on the order

blocks.text: An add-on list on the order object with a pricing loop is simpler and fine for two add-ons. Decorator wins when add-ons carry their own logic, ingredient math here, and when stacking depth matters. Say the simple option exists, then justify the pattern with the ingredient needs.
26.2 One inventory lock versus per ingredient locks
blocks.content: 26.2 One inventory lock versus per ingredient locks

blocks.text: Per ingredient locks allow more parallelism in theory, but reserving multiple ingredients in different orders risks deadlock, and the critical section is a four entry map walk. One lock is correct, simple, and fast enough by orders of magnitude.
26.3 Reserve at selection versus check at brew
blocks.content: 26.3 Reserve at selection versus check at brew

blocks.text: Checking only at brew time risks the ingredient vanishing between promise and pour. Reserving at selection makes the promise binding, at the cost of needing release() on cancellation. Binding promises are worth the compensation code.
26.4 Recipes as data versus recipe classes
blocks.content: 26.4 Recipes as data versus recipe classes

blocks.text: A class per drink lets each override behaviour, but drinks differ only in numbers, needs and price, so data rows in a book are cleaner and enable over the air menu updates. Reserve classes for drinks that genuinely behave differently.
26.5 Shared machine state versus per outlet sessions
blocks.content: 26.5 Shared machine state versus per outlet sessions

blocks.text: This design gives each outlet its own session state and shares only the inventory, which matches the hardware. A single global session would serialise customers needlessly; fully independent inventories would misstate shared containers.
A production coffee machine is a small factory, and factories run on accounting and alerts.

items: Consumption journal: every pour logs its needs map, so physical stock can be audited against sales
Low level alerts: observer thresholds per ingredient page the operator before, not after, sellout
Compensation logging: every release() is logged with its cause, because refunds are where fraud hides
Sanitation cycles: a Cleaning state on a schedule, blocking sales, mirrors real machines
Menu rollout: recipe changes are versioned data pushes, testable on one machine before the fleet
Metrics: drinks per hour, rejection reasons, and ingredient burn rates on dashboards
Testing: property test tryReserve, stock never negative under concurrent storms, plus state transition tables
Hardware watchdog: a brew that exceeds its time budget triggers the failure path automatically

blocks.text: Reserve everything or nothing, wrap add-ons as decorators, and keep the menu as data. That is the coffee machine in one line.
